findings.title: State the particle-speed condition and restore kinetic energy
draftEvidence: Modern kinetic theory makes this connection quantitatively under specified conditions, rather than assigning temperature to the speed of one particle.
In particular, it did not yet explain the relation between temperature, particle motion, and the observed heat-exchange balance.
findings.problem: The warning excludes a single particle's speed but never states the promised conditions or explains what is averaged. The source explicitly identifies kinetic energy as the missing mechanical quantity in the early theory; the English reduces that to particle motion. A child is left with an unexplained qualification rather than a usable distinction between temperature, speed and energy of motion. This is an incomplete explanation, not a finding that the existing conditional sentence is categorically false.
findings.action: In prose 4, give one explicit elementary scope, such as the classical ideal-gas model at thermal equilibrium, comparing the same kind of particles. Explain that temperature is linked to the average energy of their random motion, not one particle's speed or the bulk motion of the gas. Gloss kinetic energy as energy of motion. In prose 10, restore the source's missing kinetic-energy/temperature link as the historical difficulty. Keep paragraph 7's correct heat-as-transfer distinction.
findings.acceptance: The reader can name the model/condition, say what is averaged, and distinguish energy of motion from a single speed; the historical account explicitly retains kinetic energy.

findings.title: Restore the specific accomplishments in the Lomonosov account
draftEvidence: The note discusses work in physics, chemistry, mining, and metallurgy, as well as writing about Russian history and grammar.
He associated heat with the rotational motion of particles and used his theory to discuss melting, evaporation, and thermal conduction.
findings.problem: Writing about grammar omits the source note's specific description of him as the founder of modern Russian grammar. Discussing three phenomena also omits the source's assessment that the explanations were broadly successful. Those are distinct statements in the retained account, not merely rhetorical praise. No external historical verification is needed or claimed to identify these omissions.
findings.action: Restore the grammar role explicitly as something the textbook's note says. Restore the textbook's qualified assessment of his explanations of melting, evaporation and conduction, rather than only saying he discussed them. Keep both statements attributed to the source; keep rotation and greatest cold marked as historical theory, and retain the warning against treating absolute zero as the stopping of all microscopic motion. Preserve the conservation-anticipation caveat and the portrait contract.
findings.acceptance: The English carries the source's modern-Russian-grammar role and qualified explanatory achievement without presenting either as independently authenticated history or endorsing the rotational model as modern physics.

findings.title: Explain the terms that carry the caloric-versus-energy argument
draftEvidence: They introduced the concept of heat capacity and developed a quantitative theory of thermal conduction.
Experiments showed that frictional work could continue to warm a system as mechanical energy was supplied.
Heat and work are two ways of transferring energy, not substances contained in an object.
findings.problem: These sentences name the central achievements and rebuttal, but do not explain heat capacity, conduction, quantitative prediction, or mechanical work. Short paragraphs alone do not let the intended eight-year-old independently understand why the old theory could calculate useful results or why rubbing and working steam challenge a fixed fluid store. Caloric itself is defined clearly; the competing energy explanation needs comparable support.
findings.action: Add short inline explanations at the relevant first occurrences: conduction as heat transfer through material from warmer parts to cooler parts; heat capacity as the energy needed for a temperature rise without a change of state in the setup being compared; quantitative as making predictions with numbers; mechanical work as transferring energy when a force moves something. Use the existing rubbing and working-steam examples to connect continued effort and energy leaving the steam to those definitions. Do not invent a new historical experiment, numerical task, illustration or apparatus specification. Keep the supplied-energy and no-energy-from-nothing caveats.
findings.acceptance: The child can explain what the caloric model helped calculate and how continued rubbing and working steam involve energy transfers, using the existing examples rather than repeating unexplained technical nouns.

findings.title: Retain the measured equivalence and its mid-century timing
draftEvidence: The nineteenth-century development described here connected mechanical work with thermal energy transfer.
findings.problem: Connected is weaker than the source's explicit claim that mechanical work and heat transfer were demonstrated to be quantitatively equivalent by the middle of the nineteenth century. The following correct statement that heat and work both transfer energy does not itself convey that experimental, measurable equivalence. The rejection date in prose 11 dates the decline of caloric, not this separate result.
findings.action: Attribute the source's mid-nineteenth-century result explicitly and explain that experiments made the amounts transferred by mechanical work and heating quantitatively comparable as energy. Retain the distinction between transfer and stored internal energy, and do not turn equivalence into a claim that every engine converts all heat to work or that heating must always raise temperature.
findings.acceptance: The passage retains both the source's timing and its measurable work/heat equivalence, not just a general association, with the modern transfer caveat intact.

sourceTopicCoverage.observation: Centuries of difficult investigation, competing accounts and revision remain the opening narrative.
All four historical elements and both collisions and rubbing are retained. The four-element claim is explicitly historical.
The early seventeenth-century instrument development and its role in numerical investigation are retained as the textbook's account. No inventor, exact year or external date authentication is added.
Caloric is described as the old weightless-fluid theory, including transfer between bodies and its supposed amount/temperature relation, not a modern fluid.
The competing particle view and correct heat-as-temperature-difference transfer distinction are present; the average-motion/model condition needs N2-EN-01.
The atomic/particle connection, corpuscular name, and Newton, Hooke, Boyle and Bernoulli are retained as source-attributed history.
Text-only applicability: the English prose entry still identifies the Lomonosov portrait; no instructional data or new visual meaning is assigned. This is not an image review.

1711-1765, Russian scholar/poet/public figure, Moscow University, Pushkin's description, physics, chemistry, mining, metallurgy, Russian history and conservation anticipation are retained and attributed. Modern Russian grammar's specific founding role is missing; see N2-EN-02. Pushkin's university description is figurative, not a second literal institutional identity.

Rotation, melting, evaporation, conduction, greatest cold and reduced caloric support among Russian scholars are present. The warning that modern absolute zero does not simply stop all microscopic motion is sound. Restore the source's qualified explanatory success and explain conduction; see N2-EN-02/03.

Mid-eighteenth-century temporary caloric success, observed heat-exchange balance, inferred fluid conservation, heat capacity, numerical conduction theory and surviving terminology are present. The inference is not endorsed as universal conservation of a material heat fluid. Explain the central calculation terms; see N2-EN-03.

The early particle theory's quantitative difficulties, heat-balance problem, missing modern energy concept and caloric's temporary calculational advantage remain. The explicit kinetic-energy/temperature difficulty was generalized away; see N2-EN-01.

Late-eighteenth-century difficulties and mid-nineteenth-century rejection remain. Continued frictional heating is conditional on supplied mechanical energy, not an unlimited free source. Working steam can cool without that cooling necessarily being heat passed to another body; this does not claim all engine heat rejection vanishes. Explain work using these existing examples; see N2-EN-03.

Heat/work as energy transfers, possible internal-energy increase, no added weightless fluid and replacement of caloric conservation by energy conservation are correctly distinguished. The historical form-of-energy wording is not repeated as stored heat. Restore measured equivalence and its timing; see N2-EN-04.
